package_info.package_manager: N/A (delivered as standalone JavaScript files, not via a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (multiple unique samples, see SHA256 IOCs)
package_info.why_malicious: The JavaScript files impersonate legitimate Windows Security updates but, upon execution, initiate a fileless attack chain: they spawn a hidden PowerShell process with execution policy bypassed, delete system backups and recovery options, and download and execute the Magniber ransomware payload in memory, resulting in user data encryption and extortion. This behavior is designed to evade detection and prevent recovery, posing a severe threat to affected systems.

execution_context.trigger: user-execution (when the user opens the fake update JavaScript file)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon user-execution, the JavaScript file uses WScript.Shell to spawn a hidden PowerShell process with execution policy bypassed, passing a command to load and execute a malicious payload in memory, resulting in the initiation of a fileless attack chain.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The script leverages ActiveXObject to invoke WScript.Shell and launch PowerShell with execution policy bypassed and a hidden window, which is a common technique for malware loaders to evade user awareness and security controls.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate update scripts should use official update mechanisms and never require direct PowerShell execution, hidden windows, or execution policy bypass. They should not execute code in memory without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise IT automation may use PowerShell for deployment, but not in user-facing update prompts or with hidden execution and policy bypass.
key_indicators: Execution of PowerShell from a .js file outside browser context

execution_context.trigger: runtime (immediately after PowerShell is launched by JavaScript)
execution_context.file_location: In-memory PowerShell payload (never written to disk)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
# Pseudocode representation
powershell.exe -Command "vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet; wbadmin delete catalog -quiet; bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled No; bcdedit /set {default} bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures"
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the in-memory PowerShell payload executes system commands to delete all shadow copies, remove backup catalogs, and disable Windows recovery features, resulting in the removal of backup and restore options and increasing the impact of subsequent ransomware encryption.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of vssadmin, wbadmin, and bcdedit to delete backups and disable recovery is a well-documented ransomware tactic to prevent victims from restoring their files.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate update scripts should never interfere with or delete system backups, shadow copies, or recovery settings, as these are critical for system integrity and user data safety.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: IT administrators may use these commands for system maintenance, but never in scripts presented as user-initiated updates or without explicit administrative oversight.
key_indicators: Execution of destructive backup and recovery commands in memory

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after backup deletion, before or during ransomware payload execution)
execution_context.file_location: In-memory PowerShell or injected shellcode (never written to disk)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the PowerShell payload downloads the Magniber ransomware executable or shellcode from a remote server using WebClient, then executes it directly in memory—often via syscalls to bypass user-mode API hooks—resulting in the encryption of user files and display of a ransom note.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Downloading and executing code from an untrusted remote server, especially directly in memory, is a hallmark of advanced malware. The use of syscalls to inject shellcode further indicates intent to evade security products.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate scripts should never download and execute code from untrusted sources, nor should they perform in-memory execution or use direct syscalls for code injection.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate updaters may download signed updates, but they write to disk, verify signatures, and do not execute code in memory or use syscalls for injection.
key_indicators: Absence of written files for executed code

attack_chain.action: User is tricked into downloading and executing a JavaScript file masquerading as a Windows Security update.
attack_chain.leads_to: Initial code execution and PowerShell payload launch

attack_chain.action: The JavaScript file spawns a hidden PowerShell process with execution policy bypassed, passing a command to load the next-stage payload in memory.
The in-memory PowerShell payload deletes all shadow copies, removes backup catalogs, and disables Windows recovery features to prevent data restoration.
attack_chain.leads_to: System is left without backup or recovery options

attack_chain.action: PowerShell downloads and executes the Magniber ransomware payload directly in memory, often using syscalls to evade detection.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ransomware encrypts user files and displays ransom note

behavioral_signatures: User-initiated execution of JavaScript files outside browser context, especially with update-themed filenames
JavaScript spawning hidden PowerShell processes with execution policy bypassed
PowerShell processes executing destructive backup and recovery commands (vssadmin, wbadmin, bcdedit)
In-memory code execution and use of syscalls for shellcode injection to evade user-mode hooks
file_indicators: Unexpected .js files named to mimic Windows updates (e.g., 'Windows.Security.Update.js') in user Downloads or Desktop folders
Absence of persistent malware files on disk (fileless execution)
System missing shadow copies and backup catalogs after suspicious script execution
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests from PowerShell or JavaScript to known Magniber domains (e.g., totwo[.]pw, ittakes[.]fun, catat[.]site)
PowerShell or JavaScript making web requests to untrusted or newly registered domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for user-initiated execution of JavaScript files outside of browsers, particularly those with update-themed filenames. Alert on JavaScript processes spawning PowerShell with execution policy bypassed and hidden windows. Detect PowerShell commands that delete shadow copies, backup catalogs, or alter recovery settings. Monitor for in-memory-only malware activity and outbound connections to known Magniber infrastructure. Correlate the sudden absence of backup/restore points with recent suspicious script execution to identify potential ransomware activity.
